slides.title: Why This Tooling Matters

bullets.text: Every member re-applies the same template by hand each week — the cost is small but weekly and permanent
Hand-copying drifts: breadcrumb bars land on the wrong section, leftover placeholder text survives into the meeting
The handbooks already fix slide design (claim-based titles, one idea per slide, 24pt+), but the rules live in prose nobody re-reads
Expected outcome: the format becomes automatic, so meeting prep is spent on the argument instead of the layout

slides.notes: Motivation slide. The real claim: format compliance should not cost thinking time.

slides.title: Pipeline: Outline In, Template-Conformant Deck Out

bullets.text: Stage 1 — Outline: the model writes outline.json (roles + bullets), never raw slide geometry
Stage 2 — Assemble: each role clones its template slide, so layout, colour bar, and breadcrumb are inherited, not recreated
Stage 3 — Fill: text is replaced run-by-run, preserving the template's fonts, bullet levels, and table styling
Stage 4 — QA: schema validation against the original template, then a PDF render checked for overflow and leftover placeholders
Key design choice: the deck is never generated from scratch — the template is the only source of visual truth

slides.notes: If asked why not pptxgenjs: generating from scratch cannot reproduce the lab's breadcrumb layouts.

slides.title: Progress & Results

bullets.text: Role map complete: 22 template slides indexed by function (cover, summary, project/research/paper tracks, others)
Builder working end to end; this deck is its output, built from a 7-entry outline
Two packages shipped from one source: acm-pptx executes and emits .pptx; acm-slides-plain runs anywhere and emits the outline only
Handbook rules distilled into a reference the model loads on every run — claim-based titles, one idea per slide, no section-by-section retelling
Validation passes against the template baseline; no placeholder text survived the QA grep

slides.title: Open Problems & What I Want to Discuss

bullets.text: Portability is asymmetric: AnythingLLM has no sandbox, so the plain skill can only produce the outline — the file has to be built elsewhere
Proposed fix: treat outline.json as the contract, so any front end can start the work and any executor can finish it
Template drift: if the lab revises the template, the role map silently goes stale — worth a version field?
Question for discussion: is this worth sharing with the lab, or does per-person tooling create more maintenance than it saves?
